speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. Agent. You've mentioned episodes of unresponsiveness with facial grimacing; to begin, are these episodes sudden in onset, and do they typically last only a few seconds?

speaker: Patient
text: 7-year-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes lasting 3–4 minutes each of facial grimacing and staring over the past month. During these episodes, he is nonresponsive and does not recall them afterward. He reports a muddy taste in his mouth before the onset of these episodes. His brother witnessed him waking up, staring, and making hand gestures during one episode. The patient felt lethargic and confused afterwards.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. The duration of 3–4 minutes and the post-ictal confusion are significant; does he have any known history of head trauma, high fevers, or a family history of similar episodes?

speaker: Doctor
text:
Given the 3–4 minute duration, post-ictal confusion, and specific "muddy taste," this appears more consistent with a focal seizure than an absence seizure. Does he have any known developmental delays, speech difficulties, or witnessed events where he seemed to stare blankly for just a few seconds in the past?

REQUEST TEST: EEG (Electroencephalogram)
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Brain

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Right temporal lobe epilepsy.

The EEG results showing interictal spikes localized to the right temporal lobe, combined with the semiology of prolonged staring, impaired awareness, and post-ictal confusion, strongly support a diagnosis of focal epilepsy. The "muddy taste" is consistent with an ictal aura (gustatory phenomenon) originating in the temporal lobe. The normal MRI rules out structural lesions like tumors or significant scarring at this time.
